extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IPR practitioners, patent agents, and litigators evaluating anticipation/inherency and obviousness in inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and factual/legal standards used to determine whether prior-art disclosures (including clinical study records) anticipate or render obvious claimed methods of treatment in an IPR. Emphasizes what a person of ordinary skill would have reasonably understood or inferred from a single prior-art reference and use of expert testimony and extrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation — every claim element disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: In an anticipation analysis, the dispositive question is whether a skilled artisan would 'reasonably understand or infer' from a prior art reference that every claim limitation is disclosed in that single reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracted from Acoustic Tech., Inc. v. Itron Networked Sols., Inc. (quoting the standard). Use extrinsic evidence (declarations, depositions) to explain, but not to expand, the meaning of the reference. The petitioner must prove anticipation by a preponderance of the evidence in IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent anticipation — necessarily present characteristic
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference may anticipate without explicitly disclosing a feature if that missing characteristic is necessarily present, or inherent, in the single anticipating reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Schering Corp. v. Geneva Pharm. and related authority. The missing characteristic must be necessarily present (not merely probable). Recognition of the inherent feature in the prior art at the time is not required; skilled-artisan opinions may be used to determine the scope of the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy may be inherent in practicing claimed steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the claim includes an efficacy requirement, efficacy is inherent in carrying out the claim steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Montgomery (In re Montgomery, 677 F.3d 1375). For method-of-treatment claims, if a prior reference teaches performing the claimed steps (testing and treatment), the claimed therapeutic results may be inherent even if the outcomes were not yet reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires enabling disclosure, not reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation does not require the actual creation or reduction to practice of the prior art subject matter; anticipation requires only an enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Schering: a public disclosure that enables the claimed steps can anticipate even if the prior art did not produce reported results. Therefore, a published study protocol that enables performance of the claimed steps can anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrinsic evidence to explain but not expand prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence, such as declarations and depositions, may be considered when it is used to explain, but not expand, the meaning of a reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Baxter Travenol Labs. Expert testimony is credited to show what one of ordinary skill would have understood from the reference; however extrinsic evidence cannot add limitations not present in the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of the evidence standard in IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: The petitioner must prove invalidity (e.g., anticipation or obviousness) by a preponderance of the evidence in inter partes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the burden applied throughout the decision when assessing whether the MSR teaches every element of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction — do not import unstated exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should not be construed to exclude treating other patients when the claim does not recite any steps or limitations regarding treatment of other patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here, claim 1 recites testing a sample and treating the patient 'in response to' a determination; it does not forbid treating other patients. Therefore the presence of treatment of non-MSI-H patients in the prior art does not negate teaching of the recited steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: "In response to" in treatment claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting 'in response to determining that the colorectal cancer is MSI-H... treating the patient' does not require that only MSI-H patients be treated or that treatment never occur absent the determination, unless expressly recited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court declined to require exclusivity or an express causal-bar to other treatment; focus remains on whether the two-step sequence (test, then treat if positive) is taught.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use negation of public disclosure (Allen 13-factor analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public disclosure may be excluded from prior art under an experimental-use exception after applying a multi-factor analysis (Allen Eng'g factors) considering control by inventor, purpose of disclosure, field unpredictability, whether invention was ready for patenting, and other objective facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner bears burden to show experimental-use negation. Factors include whether publication was required by law, inventor control over the experiment, unpredictability of field (e.g., cancer), and whether inventor attempted to file earlier patent applications. Lack of evidence that inventor filed earlier undermines application of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trial protocols/public postings can be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical trial protocols posted on publicly accessible registries (e.g., ClinicalTrials.gov) can qualify as prior art and have been successfully asserted as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Salix Pharms. v. Norwich Pharms. and other precedent; publication of study record that teaches testing for a condition and treating with a drug can anticipate method claims even if trials had not yet produced data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable inference from study design and enrollment numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: A person of ordinary skill can reasonably infer procedural steps (e.g., testing before enrollment) from the circumstances of carrying out a disclosed study, such as anticipated enrollment size combined with disease incidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony may show that low incidence of a biomarker and small planned enrollment would have required pre-enrollment testing to obtain enough eligible subjects; such inferences can establish that the prior art taught the claimed steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporaneous publications to interpret scope of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications contemporaneous with or referring to the prior art study may be used to show how the skilled artisan understood the study (e.g., described as involving metastatic disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing later papers that describe the trial as 'metastatic' supports that a skilled artisan would have understood the study to involve metastatic colorectal cancer, and thus supports anticipation of claims limited to metastatic disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of clinical characteristics from eligibility language
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms in a study record such as 'tumors' or 'measurable disease' can be interpreted in context by skilled artisans to imply clinical characteristics (e.g., metastatic or unresectable disease), which can bear on whether dependent claim limitations are taught.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert testimony explaining ordinary meaning in context can be credited; opposing general medical guidelines not directly addressing the specific study do not necessarily rebut such interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human clinical data not required for patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no requirement under §101 or §112 that evidence from human clinical trials must be provided for patentability of therapeutic inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re '318 Patent and Ex parte Balzarini: absence of human trial data in an application (or prior art) does not automatically mean lack of enablement or patentability; a draftee may file without clinical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness analysis parallels anticipation when prior art fully discloses claim
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Anticipation is the epitome of obviousness' — if a reference anticipates a claim (teaches every element), the claim is also obvious over that reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in IPR Ground 2: if MSR anticipates, it is persuasive that the claims would also have been obvious over the MSR alone or with other references.
